messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Priya Shah is a 22-year-old South Asian American woman who came to treatment several months after being robbed while working a delivery shift. Late one evening, she had pulled up outside an apartment building with a food order and was still half-turned in the driver’s seat when a man yanked open her car door and ordered her out. What has stayed with her are not long, orderly memories but a few fixed moments: the door flying open, the sharp sound of his voice in her ear, the metallic jolt of panic in her chest as she froze. At times she hears that voice again in her head without wanting to, and sometimes the fear arrives in full force with no picture attached at all, just the same helpless surge that leaves her shaky and breathless. In those moments she goes back to the fact that she did not fight, did not scream, did not somehow stop it. She has come to believe this says something final about her, that she cannot protect herself and that bad things can happen to her at any time.

Since the robbery, the situations that catch Priya most quickly are ones that carry the feeling of being overpowered. Being told what to do in a sharp tone, seeing police near a parking lot or apartment complex, or noticing someone loitering and watching too closely can make her body react before she has fully thought through why. On deliveries she finds herself scanning every entrance and staircase and checking where she could run if she had to before she can tolerate getting out of the car. Even at home she wakes in the night and checks the locks, then lies there unable to settle, knowing logically she is in her room but feeling as if safety could vanish without warning. The more she lives in that keyed-up state, the more suspicious movements in other people stand out to her, so that ordinary encounters in public start to feel loaded with danger.

Her memory of the robbery feeds that vigilance. A man raising his voice in a hallway or the sight of someone approaching her car too quickly can bring back the barked command she heard that night, and with it the same bodily terror. Because the memory comes in snapshots and sounds rather than as a story with an ending, she experiences it as something that is still liable to break into the present. That leaves her braced for another attack, already identifying exits in restaurants, stores, and pickup locations before she can focus on anything else. When she cannot relax even in places she knows are safe, it confirms for her how exposed she really is.

Priya has also begun to make sense of the robbery in ways that deepen the problem. She is harsh with herself about freezing and feels she will never forgive herself for not doing more. She describes feeling different from other people her age, as if they move through the world assuming things will probably be fine while she knows they may not. That belief—that she is fundamentally unable to stop bad things from happening—makes her watchful at all times, but it also drives what she does to cope. She has started turning down delivery shifts and avoiding driving whenever she can, even riding as a passenger only when absolutely necessary. On some nights she uses drugs to dull herself enough to stop thinking and get a little sleep. At other times she tells herself the robbery was not really that bad, or almost that it did not happen the way she remembers, a private attempt to push away both the fear and the shame.

Those strategies have narrowed her life and, in turn, made the triggers more potent. Because she now avoids driving, each time she does have to get behind the wheel for work she is already tense before leaving the house, hyperaware of police cars, strangers near curbs, and anyone whose behavior seems off. The drug use gives her brief relief, but the nights she wakes alert and checks whether she is safe have not stopped. Skipping routes and deliveries has also created friction with her employer, and she feels embarrassed explaining to friends why she does not want to go out if they are driving downtown. The more isolated she becomes, the more convincing it feels that other people are separate from this kind of danger and she is not.

By the time she sought help, Priya felt trapped between constant alertness and the ways she had developed to escape it. What finally brought her in was realizing she was close to losing the delivery job she had depended on, while still feeling no safer anywhere. She says what frightens her most is that this reaction means the robber “took something permanent” from her and that she will always be the kind of person who freezes, scans for exits, and waits for the next bad thing. What she hopes, cautiously, is not to erase the event but to stop feeling as if it is still happening around every corner.
